new_statements.quote: § 18. 1. Die stärkste Betonung haben die wichtigsten Bestandteile der Rede, also im Satze diejenigen Wörter, auf denen der Nachdruck ruht, im Worte die Stammsilben, wenigstens bei einheimischen Wörtern, während uneingebürgerte Fremdwörter ihre ursprüngliche Betonung beibehalten haben. [...] 4. Ein Nebenton kommt nur in solchen schweren Zusammensetzungen vor, die auch noch als zusammengesetzt gefühlt werden. Im allgemeinen aber sind die nicht den Hauptton tragenden Silben alle gleich unbetont, zB gróusmùtər neben gróusmutər Grossmutter, bráutwùərŝt Bratwurst
new_statements.translation: §18. 1. The strongest stress falls on the most important constituents of speech: in the sentence, on those words that carry the emphasis; in the word, on the stem syllables, at least in native words, whereas unassimilated foreign words have kept their original stress. [...] 4. A secondary stress occurs only in those heavy compounds that are still felt to be compounds. In general, however, the syllables not bearing the main stress are all equally unstressed, e.g. gróusmùtər beside gróusmutər 'grandmother', bráutwùərŝt 'Bratwurst'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Germanic stem stress: primary word stress falls on the stem (root) syllable, which in native words is normally the first syllable; unassimilated loans keep source stress, but assimilated loans are shifted to initial/stem stress more readily than in Standard German (khépələ 'Kapellchen', Márkhūər 'Merkur'). Concordant statements in Schübel 1911 §22 (Stadtsteinach: 'Betont wird also wie schon im Urgerm. die erste Silbe, die im allgemeinen die Wurzelsilbe ist'), Batz 1911 §13 (Bamberg), Heilig 1898 §12 (Taubergrund) and Gerbet 1908 §124 (Vogtland).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Gebhardt §18.4: a Nebenton exists only in heavy compounds still felt as compounds (gróusmùtər ~ gróusmutər); otherwise all non-main-stressed syllables are equally unstressed. Schübel 1911 §27 likewise: Nebenton chiefly in heavy compounds whose second member is polysyllabic or long, usually on a syllable separated from the main stress by an unstressed syllable (Bróudwùorsd, Gróusmùdər, Khúnəràd).
new_statements.exceptions: Gebhardt §18.2-3: unassimilated loans keep foreign stress; tautological and comparative adjective compounds (díksát dicksatt, grósgréi grasgrün) have level stress on all members. Schübel 1911 §§23-26 (Stadtsteinach) adds: inseparable-prefix verbs stress the second element (dorchbórn durchbohren, dsərbréchn); place names conventionally stress the second member (Untersteinách, Vorderréuth); a few words shift stress to the heaviest non-initial syllable (lewéndich lebendig, Borchərmásdər Bürgermeister, Wainàchdn, Wachólder, fuchdséa fünfzehn) while Forelle, Hollunder, Un- words keep initial stress; foreign suffixes -ei, -ion, -in, -ieren are always main-stressed; no stress alternation Politík ~ Polítiker.
new_statements.domain_note: Dynamic (expiratory) word accent, treated separately from sentence accent (§18.1 covers both) and from the musical/pitch 'Silben- und Wortton' (§§19-21, one- vs two-peaked syllable accent). Examples are citation forms and compounds in the author's phonetic transcription with acute = Hauptton, grave = Nebenton.
new_statements.identity_note: Primary quote describes the city dialect of Nürnberg (Upper East Franconian; Glottolog dialect Regnitz [regn1234] under main1267). Concordant first-hand statements read for Stadtsteinach/Bamberg area (Obermain [ober1244]: Schübel 1911, Batz 1911), Taubergrund (Southwest Lower East Franconian [sout3297]: Heilig 1898) and Vogtland (Vogtlandish [vogt1234]: Gerbet 1908). Note the Glottolog reference list for main1267 wrongly includes Saarbrücken/Grossrosseln works (Pützer 1989, Steitz 1981, Schön 1922), which are Rhine/Moselle Franconian, not East Franconian.

sources.note: §18 p.14 (page image verified): strongest stress on the stem syllables of native words; unassimilated loans keep their original stress, but the dialect Germanicises assimilated loans further than the standard (khépələ Kapellchen, Márkhūər Merkur); tautological/comparative adjective compounds have level stress; a secondary stress only in heavy compounds still felt as compounds, otherwise all non-main-stressed syllables equally unstressed. §§19-21 musical (pitch) accent.

sources.note: §124 p.117 (scanned text): dynamic accent in the word as in the sentence essentially agrees with NHG; the stem = main-stress syllable stands out against pre- and post-tonic syllables more strongly than in NHG, which lose stress, quantity and vowel quality; §125 old initial stress kept in Holunder, Wacholder, Forelle; §126 loans and names forced into Germanic (initial) stress (Spitál>Sbidl, Áltar, Ártillerie, Sophie, Dorothea..); §127 place/personal names often deviate; §128-129 expiratory and musical syllable accent (one- vs two-peaked).

sources.note: §12 pp.6-7 (scanned text): 'Wie beim Satzakzent gilt auch beim Wortakzent der Satz, dass die wichtigsten Bestandteile den Ton erhalten. Daher ist die Stammsilbe sehr stark betont im Gegensatz zu den sie umgebenden Neben- und Endsilben, die entweder unbetont oder nebenbetont erscheinen.' Anm.: compound stress as in NHG; tautological compounds level-stressed. (Gebhardt's §§13-18 explicitly modelled on Heilig.)
